Okay, its a bug.

Why it creates different queries? Because we added `limit 1` to `findOne` to prevent additional stuff loading. Currently, in query builder "special distinct-based query" is used in the case if either limit or offset is defined. In this case we don't need this special query, but this is too complex to resolve right now, and we already have a different relation load mechanizm in 0.3.0.

But the actual bug is in query we had even in 0.2.9. It shouldn't select columns from two tables with same names. I have fixed that.
Published it under `@rc`, its a breaking bug, but its not super urgent since issue reproduces only when using custom join column names. `npm i typeorm@0.2.12-rc.1`

issue.body:
Hi there!

### Context

I just made a small Pull request to address https://github.com/typeorm/typeorm/issues/3118. Postgres has a ([built-in](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html#SQL-SYNTAX-IDENTIFIERS)) limit of 63 characters for the name of columns and aliases used in SQL queries.

This prevent TypeORM from being able to properly transform **raw results** to Entities when querying "deeply nested" relations, as it can generate aliases as long as `"CategoryWithVeryLongName__postsWithVeryLongName__authorWithVeryLongName_firstName"` (dummy example, but still 81 characters long).

Thus, the "populated" (joined) `authorWithVeryLongName` is never converted from a raw result to an entity (and stays `undefined`).

### Solution

A similar issue has already been addressed for Oracle [here](https://github.com/typeorm/typeorm/blob/c051810bfaaf8781e28f251754ba8eb4dc922cce/src/query-builder/SelectQueryBuilder.ts#L1932) by abbreviating the name of the selected column.
My concern with this code is that when `alias` is `"CategoryWithVeryLongName__postsWithVeryLongName__authorWithVeryLongName"` and `columnName` is `"firstName"`, abbreviating `"firstName"` to 2 characters might create collisions with other columns starting with `"fi"`.
That's why I decided to write `shorten`, which is focused on shortening **aliases**.

I also added a test which guarantees that `authorWithVeryLongName` is correctly loaded/instantiated as an entity.

### Why

Some E2E tests started failing in our application when [this fix](https://github.com/typeorm/typeorm/issues/3350) was introduced. Using `__` instead of `_` (as a separator for the path of tables) lengthened the selection aliases.

Any feedback is most welcome, this is only my second PR in the project. Thanks.

issue.title: Duplicate aliases guarantee data corruption

**Steps to reproduce or a small repository showing the problem:**

I am running into a rather significant, code-breaking problem that is forcing our team to reevaluate whether we'll be able to use TypeORM at all. In multiple cases so far, even after just a week or two of building queries, we have run into a problem that guarantees that we will end up with corrupt data in the database.

The auto-generated aliases, which TypeORM does on its own and allegedly has to do, can create duplicate aliases. This means that data can literally end up in the wrong field, and a delete-by-database-id-number will end up deleting the wrong one.

Here is an example of the problem:

SELECT "COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_REQUEST"."COMMITTEE_ID" **AS "COMM_COMMITTEE_ID",** "COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_REQUEST"."PHASE" AS "COMM_PHASE", "COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_REQUEST"."COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_SESSION_ID" AS "COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_REQUEST_COMM", "COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_REQUEST"."REQUEST_DATE" AS "COMM_REQUEST_DATE", "COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_SESSION"."COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_SESSION_ID" AS "COMMITTEE_APPROVAL_SESSION_COMM", "COMMITTEE_DECISION_LOG"."DECISION" AS "COMM_DECISION", "COMMITTEE_DECISION_LOG"."COMMITTEE_ID" **AS "COMM_COMMITTEE_ID",**

Despite these being completely different values, they are given the same alias, meaning they will have the same value when they shouldn't. IDs end up wrong. Deleting or updating or retrieving a database record will be wrong. We won't know it's happening, because TypeORM doesn't register this as an error. We will simply have incorrect data in the database until someone runs into it and notices something is wrong and we will have to manually correct it field-by-field along with all associated data wherever it may be. It is a worst-case-scenario and we don't feel we can take a single step forward relying on this product unless this issue is addressed.

After searching for a while, it seems this is a known issue, and has been for a while, which is even more confusing. The solutions suggested have been:

1) Use shorter aliases. This would be fine, except 100% of the team needs to know about this 100% of the time and never make a mistake, ever. And if their shorter aliases produce an overlap on their own and it is missed, we will end up with corrupt data in the database and have to track it down and change it manually. We have to check manually, on every query, for any duplicate, and never, ever, ever fail.

2) Use shorter column names. With an enterprise application already in place, this is simply not an option.

Neither of these seem very sufficient to me. Seeing this in action for the first time was rather shocking, as it is a guaranteed problem that will be extremely difficult to solve, long after a LOT of damage has been done. It is confusing to me that this is a known issue and has not been resolved.

My team has discussed downgrading to a previous version of TypeORM, back when alias names were allowed to be extremely long; my understanding is that the the reason they were shortened is so they would work with Oracle's alias length limit, but this has only made data corruption inevitable, which seems like an even worse problem. So we could downgrade, but then we'll never know if we can upgrade to the next version. My suggestion has been to contact TypeORM directly, as solving this problem seems like a necessity, and not something we should hack together with a roundabout method.

It seems to me that the solution is simple. When generating the aliases, keep track of the aliases that have been generated in the query up to that point. If there is another alias that would be a duplicate of an existing one, simply change a letter on the end to a random, different one. Repeat.

This seems like it would solve this problem completely, and would be rather simple. But we'd really like to see it addressed, because as far as we can tell, it is a massive, stop-everything-right-now type of problem that we refuse to implement, and no one else on the planet should either. We don't want to wait, and spend months on development, hoping someday it'll be fixed.

Others on the team have pointed out that we can't rely on TypeORM's team to implement a solution in a reasonable amount of time, as it may take months, or years, so we should just drop it and look for something else, no matter how much else we like it. But this seems like a problem that should be solved for everyone, not just us. What can be done?
